newsitem.title: USA: US firms can cut workplace violence risk - experts.
newsitem.headline: US firms can cut workplace violence risk - experts.

text.p: In 1982, an International Business Machines Corp employee was shot and killed at his North Carolina office by a former employee of the company.

Incidents such as this are a serious problem for U.S. companies, but there are measures they can take to reduce the risk of such devastating workplace violence, experts at the Risk and Insurance Management Society (RIMS) conference here told risk managers.

"There are a lot of reasonable, cost effective things a company can do to reduce the risk of an incident of violence," said Patrick King, who was responsible for security at the IBM plant where the shooting took place.

"I had the unfortunate experience of witnessing a friend die from a gun shot in a plant where I had the security responsibility," said King, who now is the south-east region business development manager for American Protective Services Inc, a privately-held contract security service in Morrisville, North Carolina.
"No one had to tell me 'don't let it happen again.'"
Revenge is often a motive for workplace violence, said Thomas Lekan, senior vice president and director of corporate security for Keycorp in Cleveland.
And, although the desire for revenge against a manager or company can lead to homicide, it also can take the form of theft, vandalism or a lack of productivity, he told the conference.
The first and easiest thing companies can do to reduce the risk of such violence is to screen carefully job applicants before they are hired, King said.

Thorough, legal background and reference checks can often turn up red flags, such as patterns of intimidating behaviour, problems with a previous employer or a string of drunk driving arrests, he said.
In addition, people who work in highly technical fields often tend to be among those who are most susceptible to violence as a result of losing their jobs, Lekan said.
"In both hiring and firing, do your homework," Lekan said.

A number of states have now revised their laws so that a company that discusses a former employee's behaviour on the job with a potential employer will not be guilty of discriminating against that individual, he said.
And preventive measures such as careful hiring, he said, are far more effective than physical security measures, such as fences, guards and electronic monitoring devices.
Companies also should not tolerate aggressive behaviour by employees once they are hired.
Intimidating, threatening, belligerent acts and words are sufficient indicators of a problem to trigger an appropriate response, King said.
Workplace violence often starts with shouting, moves to shoving and then later to shooting, he said.
"When a company tolerates intimidating, aggressive behaviour from anyone, they are sending the message that it's okay to be a bully," King said.
"Why should this be acceptable in any work environment," he asked.
The warning signs also are often picked up by other employees. In almost every instance of workplace violence, King said, co-workers knew there was a problem.
Punitive actions, he said, must be based on a standard of acceptable conduct, not how long someone has been around or how well they are liked.
And once a policy or code of conduct has been established, companies must be consistent in enforcing it, he said.
The consequences of failing to address this issue can be devastating, resulting in the loss of life and even the loss of the business.
"Once there has been an incident, nothing is ever the same," he said. "It never leaves you."
A prominent Californian law firm was forced to close after a gunman shot and killed eight of its employees in 1993, he said.
The other employees, he said, no longer wanted to work for the firm, and clients did not want to do business there.
"There is no price you will pay to prevent an incident of violence that will exceed what you will pay if you do nothing and one happens," he said.
